utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, everyone. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, registrar. We are -- today Thursday. I would like to greet all the people present in the courtroom, Prosecution representative, Defence counsel, the accused, and Mr. Coric who is back in court. I will ask the registrar to move into private session for a few minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, as far as procedural matters are concerned, Ms. Nozica and Mr. Murphy have filed a motion which we got yesterday. The Prosecution will reply in writing, I assume, will reply to this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I take on board it doesn't seem to be particularly urgent in the sense that -- but we will file in the usual time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I asked you the question, but it's quite obvious that you were going to respond. I shall now indicate to both parties that according to our calculations, and the registrar will intervene if I've made a mistake, Defence teams should have another 30 minutes, if I'm not mistaken. Registrar is nodding to indicate that I am right. So I shall give you the floor so that you can resume your cross-examination. Mr. Ibrisimovic, you would like to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to be specific about what you said, you said the Defence had a total of 30 minutes left. Is that in reference to all the remaining Defence teams or just Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a very good question, Mr. Ibrisimovic. This is why I shall turn to the registrar once again and to ask him where we stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registrar has just told me that what I was led to believe. With the extra 30 minutes, that would amount to six hours. So theoretically, other Defence counsel don't have any more time left, unless of course additional time is given to you. Mr. Ibrisimovic, how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, we allowed the prior Defence to use half our time, so I was counting on our 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank my learned friend Mr. Ibrisimovic for this question. I wanted to have the point clarified myself. I know that General Petkovic's Defence have used up more than our one hour, but our learned friend, Mr. Karnavas, promised to allow us to use half his time if necessary. Therefore, I would ask the Chamber to allow the Petkovic Defence another half hour should the Chamber deem the questions being asked to be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber realises that some Defence counsel haven't taken the floor yet. Mr. Pusic, Mr. Ibrisimovic, Mr. Coric's Defence counsel who has not taken the floor, but I think he's given his time to someone else, and Mr. Karnavas, who -- Mr. Prlic's Defence counsel has not taken the floor either I know he's given some of his time to others. The Trial Chamber has discussed the matter and with a degree of flexibility rules that Defence teams will have an extra hour from now onwards. So you may decide how you share the time given that Mr. Ibrisimovic has said that he would -- he needs 30 minutes or he would like to have 30 minutes. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I would just like to say one thing about the transcript. The President did indeed remember this well. We allowed the Stojic Defence team all of our time so we have no questions for our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning Mr. President Your Honours at this point in time I do not see any cross-examination. There maybe five or 10 minutes, I don't know, I but think point from what I've seen so far I don't see the use of going over old territory that has been gone over so far, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just not sure I understand. There is a total of one hour now or is there a half hour plus an extra hour? I don't understand the "total of one hour."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's one hour in total. The remaining 30 minutes, which will amount to six hours, plus another 30 minutes. So there will only be 30 minutes more.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, theoretically you will have between 25 and 30 minutes, and Mr. Ibrisimovic will have 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Greetings to all.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another question about the 9th of May, 1993, Witness. Can you please go to my set of documents and look up document number 4D 00552. This is a document dated the 10th of May, 1993. This is the operations duty officer of the 4th Corps, and he sends this to the BH army and to the president of the BH Presidency, Alija Izetbegovic. As we have very little time left, can we please just try to focus on two sentences. The beginning of the first paragraph, which reads: "On the 9th of May, 1993, an unexpected general attack of the HV and HVO forces was launched against the BH army - the command of the 4th Corps and the 41st glorious motorised brigade." And then the first sentence in paragraph 4, please, which reads: "During Ustasha attacks, the attacks of the Ustasha units on the command and the logistics of the 4th Corps and the 41st Glorious Motorised Brigade, one combatant was killed by two members of the HV from Split, two were seriously wounded, and two were arrested while two are listed as missing." My question, Witness: This sort of description provided by the duty operations officer to the 4th Corps and to the president of the Presidency, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, do you consider this sort of description to be an accurate one with regard to what happened on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: No? All right. Unfortunately, I have no time now to ask you why not, since as far as I understand you were not yourself in Mostar on your day. Therefore, you didn't witness what happened. Is my understanding correct? You were in fact not in Mostar on the 9th of May, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 9th of May I was above the hill in Mostar. I was viewing it. But there are details in this report that I can neither confirm nor deny, so therefore I can't say it is a -- whether it's an accurate report or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, my question was not in reference to the entire report but, rather, in reference to the allegation made to the Supreme Commander of the BH army. There's these two sentences containing this one allegation, the HVO on that day attacked the command of the 4th Corps and the brigade command. That is the allegation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is also the allegation that the HV was involved, and at this stage I -- certainly I don't believe that was ever reported from the UN side. And also the details that you read out about the HV from Split, there's no way we were able to get into -- know any details about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, sir, you are in fact entirely right. When I was asking my question, what I was really half was the first sentence that we read and the beginning of the second sentence, which is the description of the attack itself as an attack on the building housing the command of the 4th corps and the brigade command. So this is the only part of the report that I'm really after since unfortunately I know you can't confirm or deny anything about the other elements contained therein. We know you had no such information. Therefore, all I'm focusing on is this one allegation contained in this report. Can you confirm that allegation as an accurate one, or did you deny its authenticity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe it was confirmed by the United Nations that in fact the attack started at that position, albeit I believe that was indicated at the time, but if you recall we were not present when the attack started, and by the time we were able to get in -- in a location where we could view the -- the action, the fighting was possibly a little bit more widespread.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Would it be a correct assumption based on your answer that you don't really know how the attack commenced on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Let us move on to my next topic. If you remember the end of our exchange yesterday, you confirmed that what was going on not only in the Sector South, which you covered, but also in Central Bosnia, was all interconnected, and that what was going on in Mostar at the time could not be fully understood unless one understood also what was going on in other parts of the is sector as well as the neighbouring sector, that of Central Bosnia. It is for this purpose I want us to go to go through a document, but I think this document requires private session since the document is a protected one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, would you please say it again? It will only take a few minutes -- or a few seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I'll give the Reader's Digest version. We thank the gentleman for coming to The Hague we thank the gentleman for coming here to give his evidence. We do wish to point to the Trial Chamber that we only question witnesses when we deem it absolutely necessary, and we're very judicious, and therefore we would appreciate that when we do we ask for additional time with certain witnesses that the Court -- the Trial Chamber take our attitude into consideration in granting more time, because I believe we have been very judicious over the past few months or I would say since the beginning of the trial. In any event, that's it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the Prosecution have redirect before the Judges put their questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, a couple of questions, but I'm afraid we'll have to go back into private session for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a question. Is it possible to give the witness again a copy of that map 1:10000 of Mostar that was used previously? I note that the sign has disappeared, but is that possible? This map. I hoped it would still be there. I hesitate to give this one because I have made signs on it, but if there is no other copy available, perhaps that will do. I will also furnish the witness with a makeshift compass, which is 10 centimetres long, as will be shown, and I would like the witness to draw a circle of 1 kilometre around the place where the house was where he lived. If this could be brought to him, please. I have roughly marked the area where I thought the witness had said that the house was, but of course you are not in any way bound by this. I would like you to perhaps in red mark where the house was, where you think the house was, which was your HQ.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think you should have the needle on the house as it were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now could you show us where Tito Most is on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And perhaps you also encircle it. And Spanski Trg, the Spanish Square?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Okay. So would the conclusion of this be, Mr. Finlayson, that the distance from your house to the Spanish Square would be 1.000 and not 1.500 metres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be the conclusion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Perhaps you want to -- to put the date on -- on the map and then sign it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Could you also -- yes. Perhaps it would be useful if you would mark the place where your house is in the red circle with a 1. I think that the red marker is the most effective one, actually. And you can draw large figures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Then the Tito Most with a 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And the Spanish Square with a 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, an IC number, Mr. Registrar, for the map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this map will become IC 551.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, usually or normally I would have asked my question at the very beginning of your testimony, but I did not want to interrupt you, so I refrained from it. It's a very simple question. When you introduced yourself, you gave your rank. Lieutenant commander, that was. I know that in principle UNMOs were non-commissioned officers, or they could have been also higher-ranking officers. And you also said that you were a driver at some point in time. So I'd like to have some clarification on this regarding the exact title of your rank, taking by way of reference the NATO nomenclature, and I would like exactly -- to know exactly what your position was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. The UNMO position in the -- in this mission, the United Nations military observer is always an officer and only an officer of major, lieutenant colonel, or captain rank. They are only -- that is the only -- the only ranks in the United Nations military observer organisation. It runs as its own organisation. It doesn't have a support network of non-commissioned officers or soldiers. Therefore, when you join, your rank -- everyone has to -- if you're familiar with the term "muck in," everyone has to do all the jobs. So yes, you had to do driving tasks. One day you might be a driver. When I day a driver, you might be tasked with driving. On other days -- on the very next day you may be the duty officer in the headquarters. So it's only officers, and it's only officers working together. They are funded differently and they are operated differently than the -- sorry, yeah. The battalions, they work together. They don't get a lot of support. Ideally you have to find your own accommodation. That's -- that was the general run of the mill. My mission was to go into East Mostar and set up a team. I was given an unarmoured vehicle, a hand-held radio, and two people, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If you allow a follow-up. You said two people. Before you said there were no soldiers. What do you mean by two people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two fellow UNMOs. When I went into East Mostar to set up that team is what I was talking about. I had a Danish captain and an Argentinian lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And what would your rank be in -- in general army terminology? Because I recall you had some sort of superior lieutenant, but lieutenant is normally the lowest officer grade. That's what may confuse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the -- in the navy, a lieutenant commander is a major.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to go to the 9th of May, since it is a relevant date, and I'd like to go back to document 4D 00552. It is a portion of a book published by Mr. Esad Sejtanic. It was the last document in the binder that you were provided with. This document is a report by the duty officer Emir Besalic [phoen] and oddly enough it is sent to the supreme commander in Sarajevo and to Mr. Izetbegovic in person. It is rather astonishing to see that a duty officer could send something directly to the Supreme Commander of the army. But this being said, in the first paragraph he described the surprise attack on the 9th of May, providing details as well. Towards the middle of the sentence it is stated that there were 120-millimetre mortars, howitzers, and tanks, and I see "tanks" in the plural. So let me talk about the tanks, because I do recall you saying a few days ago that on the 9th it of May you had attempted to enter Mostar, unsuccessfully, and that you went to position yourself on an OP to have an overview, and that next to it, adjacent to it, there was a tank. Can you confirm today that from the place where you were next to the OP there was a tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How could you distinguish that tank from, say, an ABiH tank, provided they had any, or was there an insignia or a chequer-board or anything that would lead you to believe that this was an HVO tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At this point in time I can't recall exactly what incidents there. I'm fairly sure there was one, and we also talked to the troops that were on that tank. We actually had to pass the tank to -- to go to the position where we ended up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very Well. So you talked to the men in the tank. And I also understood that this tank fired. Is that what you said? I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that tank fired, and it seems a remarkable thing that I can't recall, but I don't believe it -- it fired. The tank that was firing was the tank more -- was -- that was closer to the city centre. We were fairly well to the north. And that tank stood quiet for most of the day, if not all the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the tank stood quiet. But you mention another tank, that one fired. Where was it positioned, that other tank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That tank was fired more or less under -- the -- I marked it up on a map, but using that map that we were looking at before, it was roughly to the west of the -- due west of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. When that tank fired, did you see it yourself with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Affirmative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Back to the document, because if I took it out, I wanted to establish a correlation between that report and the tank. It is said in the document that there was artillery fire on the -- on the ABiH positions. In Mostar, did you know where those ABiH positions were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Essentially we -- as -- as was mentioned earlier or what was considered in -- as the starting point was where the headquarters were. We could make out where the majority of the fighting seemed to -- to be occurring, and -- and as the day went on, it did tend to move towards the east bank slightly. It certainly wasn't an accurate observation, but from memory that's what -- what we could see. So you could see where -- obviously where the tank rounds were going in. Very -- reasonably localised along the -- what -- more or less the Bulevar area. It's a very loose area. Unfortunately I've got some photos of it, but they're in New Zealand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are a navy major. Well, in the navy, you also have guns. You can shoot guns from ships. So you must be experienced with firing. When a tank fires, is it randomly, or does it aim at particularly -- particular objectives that were assigned to the tank on the basis of a preliminary plan or based on observations by the leader of the team in the tank, or is it through a radio relay? Is he given the coordinates for shooting the firing charge that way? So based on that, when the tank would fire, would it fire at specific objectives or was it a bit sort of randomly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the tank rounds were -- were fairly localised, as I said, so they appeared to be, and I would expect them to be at a -- at a known target, either from an observer or from a higher command order. Like they weren't -- the rounds weren't landing in a large pattern. The fighting was -- there was pretty much a focused area of fighting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may assist in the question. Would you agree that while artillery fire often is ordered to cover a certain surface, the tank is used to hit spots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours. Your Honours, my apologies indeed. This objection may not be entirely appropriate, but I think it's my duty to raise it. I don't think it's a good idea for Judges to be asking leading questions simply because of facts of human nature. And when one is asked something by a Judge, one is prone to confirm whatever the substance is of Judge's leading question. Therefore, I think it might be a wise idea to avoid this in future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, how was there a leading question by the Judges?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the very fact that the questions -- that the question begins by asking, "Would you agree with" something. This implies the Judge's own position, that this would be the case, and based on experience, we can conclude that when asked such questions by one of the Judges the witnesses are more likely to agree simply because it seems like an appropriate thing to agree with a Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A clever observation, Ms. Alaburic, of course. Funny also to a certain extent. I've seen a bit of laughter. You're quite aware of the fact, of course, that this was just assuming up question because the substance of the answer had entirely been given by the witness in answer to Judge Antonetti's question, and it was just assuming up of an answer that was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, and I don't want to belabour the point, but frankly I don't believe that a foundation has been laid with respect to this gentleman as to whether he's competent to even answer that question. He was in the navy. He is an officer, but he was an engineer, as I understand it. He might have had some training before going to Bosnia but that training was limited to observation. So I am not suggesting the gentleman is not an expert; however, I believe a foundation would need to be laid such as, what is your actual training with respect to tanks, and so on and so forth. So -- but in any event, I don't -- I believe Ms. Alaburic is correct and -- but in any event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, well, I was sure you were going to see this, because I asked him as a marine -- as a navy officer did he have any officer in firing in artillery fire, and he didn't say no. So we could put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President but he didn't answer that part because if you look at your question, and I -- and I paid very close attention to it, there was a -- an assumption that you made, and of course the gentleman didn't say, "Yes, I have a lot of experience," he went to answer your question. So maybe he does have the experience, but he didn't actually answer the question, but I agree that you did try to lay the foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's going to answer. Yes, Mr. Witness, you followed this exchange. This is a forensic issue which may be futile to you, but everything that is said here is relevant. So back to it. You were a navy officer. Did you have any personal experience in New Zealand in the navy forces of your country of artillery fire from a ship? You have some knowledge and expertise, but based on that could you make any observations as to what was happening in Mostar when there was -- when there were tank rounds?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my -- my training in the navy when I first joined was all associated with the control -- control mechanisms behind anti-aircraft artillery and guided missiles. Later as I was a commissioned officer, I was responsible for all weapon systems on board a frigate. However, the -- the tanks, specific knowledge of tanks, is -- is minimal. However, having said that, the basics are the same. If the bullet lands in the one place, you assume it's being aimed at that location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that the basics were the same. Can we conclude from that that when there is firing from a ship or from a tank the same basics apply? You have to have the coordinates of the objective. You have to have the degree of angle for the gun. Do you find the same basics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The same basics certainly apply. In this particular case the range was exceptionally short, so those calculations were probably a little bit simpler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes. We have a specialist who is going to put a question to you. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I had intended to ask this when my turn came, but I'd like to ask permission from the Trial Chamber to go ahead and ask it now because this is a very important question, and if you won't allow me to ask the question then you can ask it, and this is my question: At what time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Does this question have something to do with the questions of a technical nature that were put or not? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Yes, of a technical nature. Yes, a technical question. In view of point 25 of the witness statement where it says that, "While we were observing, one tank --" Judge Trechsel, it is the time I'd like to refer to. When the witness arrived in that place whether he found the tank already there or whether the tank came afterwards. And if there wasn't a tank, why the tank arrived afterwards. So these are very important questions, whether the operation was prepared or not, because the witness says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That is not the issue, Mr. Praljak. The issue is that we have the direct -- first interrogation direct, then cross, then redirect, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. The procedure in this Tribunal is that the parties are allowed to ask follow-up questions from the Judges' questioning, and then the Prosecution is usually given the last word, and I think that General Praljak wishes to ask a question based on a question that was raised by Judge Antonetti, and so therefore it would fit within the proper mode of a follow-up based on information elicited from the Trial Chamber. So I think in this instance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: What is the Prosecution's view on this? I'm very sorry if I've misstated the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just -- I think the basic point here is that this has gone on and on, and you can't go on, on a free for all, forever. If there is any follow-up questions to the question put by the president, it was not this question. The question put by the president was talking about targeting, use of a tank for direct -- what's called direct fire, as opposed to indirect fire, and Mr. Praljak is now going off on a whole different angle about who -- when the tank showed up, and that's not proper follow up to the Judge's question under any scenario, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me just briefly respond to that, because again and I'll try to be as -- let me take a deep breath first because I think this is misleading on the part of the Prosecution. Your Honour, you wanted to ask about the tank. The question is when did the tank -- when did the tank arrive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The gentleman wishes to ask that question to clarify it, because I think it's relevant to your question. Your follow-up questions afterwards had to do with what was being targeted. So in fairness to General Praljak and for the purposes of understanding the record, I think when that tank arrived it arrived at the 8th? At the 9th? At the 10th? At what point in time? Now, the gentleman may know or he may not know, but I think that's relevant, and I think that's what the gentleman wishes to ask. And I think we just should be able to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this tank, was it there before you arrived or was the tank brought in after your arrival? This is a very simple question. No point in wasting too much time on this. Did -- was it there before or after?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both the tank that we were positioned alongside and the tank that was doing the majority of the firing were there when we arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The tank was positioned there before you got there. This is what you say, line 3, page 39; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I've lost my copy, but, yes, that is correct, and earlier I mentioned the tank we were next to we passed. We had to get around the back of it to get to our location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please. In paragraph 25 of the statement, it says: "While we were watching, an HVO tank stopped immediately next to us." So if they were observing and the tank stopped, then it's that tank that came afterwards. "There was an HVO tank right beside us while we were observing," was the sentence. And it is quite right for Judge Antonetti to see, for example, how far the tank was, one and a half kilometres or what the distance was. And now why -- if the tank was there, why didn't it take part in the operation straight away? Why didn't it shoot straight away?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in light of your statement at line 25, I think there is a discrepancy which General Praljak has noted. In your written statement, you seem to indicate that this tank has parked alongside where you stood. In other words, this would mean that the tank arrived afterwards, whereas a while ago you said -- but in any event, we're talking about two tanks. Which tank are you talking about, was it the tank that remained there all the time and which was brought in afterwards, or are you talking about the other tank, the one that fired the shots? Now, in paragraph 25, which tank does this relate to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I haven't got that in front of me, but both tanks were in position when we arrived on site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Maybe there is another problem in translation. I -- I suppose that this statement was taken in English. So this is the original text, and here it says: "We --" I'm quoting from point 25 on page 5, the second -- third sentence: "We managed to find a route or route that enabled us to come in from the northern direction to a position about West Mostar to the north. We had binoculars and were able to observe the open hostilities occurring in the city. There was an HVO tank right beside us while we were observing." There is no mention here of the tank driving up. So maybe it was not well translated or it was misread in the Croatian, but there is no foundation whatsoever for the question that Mr. Praljak has now put.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, while we're on the subject of the tank, and I think it is an important question, the question that the witness was asked before was left out. What time did he arrive at that location? Because you see from the statement that he came in a round about route. So knowing the territory, he couldn't arrive before 12.00 noon or 1.00 p.m. So perhaps it's important to know when he arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At what time, then, was it? At what time did you get there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The gentleman is probably correct. I can't recall the exact time, but because we had been -- had so many problems trying to get into the town through our normal route and then a second alternate route, I seem to remember it was before lunchtime, but not a great deal before lunch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, before noon, before 1.00?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's all we can say about this matter, i.e., paragraph 25. If there are no further questions, then I'd like to thank you, Witness, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, for having come to testify at the request of the Prosecution. I wish you a safe journey home, and I would like the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, the witness you had scheduled for this week have now finished their testimonies. Everything is under control for next week, I believe, is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That completes the evidence for this week and the witness has scheduled for Monday appears to be on schedule with no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I just have a brief request, Your Honours. With respect to Alija Lizde, that was the previous witness, the Prosecution filed a letter or a memo or something to the effect regarding our submissions, our evidence. I would like until tomorrow to respond to that. I should have it later on in the afternoon, but I would like tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like extra time to be able to respond, is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your request has been granted, Mr. Karnavas. I'd like to thank all the people present in the courtroom and invite you to come back to our next hearing, which will be on Monday at a quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 14th day of May, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.46 a.m,
